name: Adam Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I feed steel into a washing-machine panel press and check every run for cracks or dents. I help the setter change dies but keep clear until the press is isolated. I have a vocational certificate and years on the line, yet my pay is on the low side for an operator.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life at home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ingrid cleans at the primary school; our son Erik and daughter Freya are both school age, and we have a mortgage. We have less than a month saved and few similar plants nearby. I sometimes use an AI app for under-twelves football drills, once I have seen another coach get a useful result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stamping crew that the press still needs a person to spot a split panel. The AI excitement can settle down as far as I am concerned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant might stay ordinary, but our mortgage does not become easy. Ingrid cleans at the primary school, and our two small wages leave less than a month saved for the children or a car repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep feeding and checking the press on my paid shift and coach the under-twelves on Tuesday. I would keep using my AI app for football drills and ask when the next paid setter apprenticeship opens; an enquiry is all I can make without an offered place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about our thin cash margin, though the press work itself feels familiar. Ingrid keeps the accounts in a notebook and sees every short week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How often do you use the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once every few weeks when I need a new warm-up drill. That is an old habit, not training for work or a new skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the setter apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setter changes dies safely and earns more than I do. I have a vocational certificate, but I would need a real paid apprenticeship place before touching that job.

I would let **AI excitement** settle while work stays ordinary.
think: Our **mortgage** remains difficult even if AI stalls.
Ingrid’s **school wage** and mine leave less than one month saved.
do: Feed and check **press panels** on paid shifts.
Keep using the **football app** for existing coaching drills.
Ask when a **paid setter apprenticeship** actually opens.
feel: **Anxious** about household cash despite familiar work.

fieldNote: Adam’s occasional **AI app use** is an existing football habit, not work training.

steps.text: Keep feeding and checking panels on paid press shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lads the company can buy better scheduling, but it owes loyal operators a fair shot at the new jobs. I would say apprenticeships beat a leaflet about innovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first hours to disappear could be feeding and checking, the parts of my shift a robot can copy. The setter might last longer, but only a real training place and enough pay would help us keep the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring my two recent rosters to the shift manager and apply for the next funded setter apprenticeship if it offers paid time and guarded practice. If accepted, I would enrol; once I finish it and a reachable setter post is advertised at bill-covering pay, I would apply; if there is no place, I would check local postings without waiting for an hours cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, like waiting for a loose tackle. The plan has stages, and the manager has promised none of them yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start running the new robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after an offered paid practice slot with an isolated press and a qualified setter beside me. Watching a demonstration from the aisle would not teach me the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an evening course instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now. Ingrid’s wage and mine barely meet the mortgage, so I would first look for an employer-funded place with paid time.

think: Robots could remove **feeding hours** before setter work.
A **funded place** and adequate job would have to protect our mortgage.
do: Apply for a **funded setter apprenticeship** with paid time and safe practice; enrol only if accepted.
Apply after **qualification** only to a posted reachable bill-covering setter role.
Check **local postings** if no training place is offered.
feel: **Anxious** because each useful stage remains uncertain.

fieldNote: Adam is **open to proven change**, but refuses unpaid or unguarded practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the football parents that thinking AI might arrive in 2028 when I am forty-five and capable press robots around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A foreign owner could install them faster than our team can learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most feeding shifts to vanish before I get a setter ticket. We have a mortgage and less than a month saved, and I wake up wondering which child’s expense gets missed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel our planned holiday and ask the plant for written staffing dates. If my paid shifts end, I would apply for posted reachable maintenance or factory work only where the wage covers our bills and safe instruction is offered; if nothing adequate is posted, I would ask the lender about a temporary payment plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed; losing most of my wage soon would put the house in danger. Coaching the children would keep me useful, but it would not pay the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would odd jobs be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could repair a neighbour’s gate if asked, but I cannot budget a mortgage on occasional favours. I would report any actual pay and still seek a proper posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the setter apprenticeship still help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a funded paid place opens quickly and a posted role survives at enough pay. I would not call a course an escape when the press team is disappearing.

I would question **rapid foreign-owner installation** at the plant.
think: I expect **most feeding shifts** to vanish before qualification.
Our **tiny reserve** cannot protect the children’s costs and mortgage.

feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless household worry.

fieldNote: He expects **major feeding-hour loss** after the capable robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the break room that thinking AI in 2031 and capable press robots around 2034 give us five years. The company should spend those years on paid apprenticeships, not speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I would still have the mortgage and school costs. Setter work might buy time if a real local post survives, but an evening certificate without a vacancy would use money we cannot spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for the next fully funded setter apprenticeship with paid shift time and an isolated-press practice place. If accepted, I would enrol and learn the robot controls with a qualified setter, then apply for a posted reachable setter job at a wage that covers our bills; if no place opens, I would search posted local factory jobs at that wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but there is time to test a proper route. I would not put our mortgage on a course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, only the app for football drills. I would learn actual press controls if the employer offered safe paid practice after another setter showed that system works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ingrid support the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if my paid hours continued and the course cost us nothing. She would not agree to pay tuition while our reserve covers less than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that thinking AI in 2036 and capable press robots around 2039 leave thirteen years for proper apprenticeships. Management should publish places and wages instead of telling operators to be patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when the thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots might handle panels. Our children may be grown, but the mortgage balance, Ingrid’s school hours and my health cannot be guessed from today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep my press shifts and put a new amount from each full wage month into savings after bills. In the first year after 2036, if I still work there, I would compare actual rosters and posted jobs; after sustained cuts, I would apply only to reachable safe work paying enough for our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious about today’s money, though the distant date is less sharp. I would rather ask the manager for dates than pretend a decade guarantees me a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not have figures that would let me promise that. I would review the mortgage and pension with Ingrid when the children are older, then decide based on actual income and health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to keep using my football-drill app now and then. That habit is not the same as learning the plant’s robot controls or being offered a setter post.

I would separate **2036 systems** from 2039 press robots.

Children growing older do not guarantee **school wages** for Ingrid.
do: Keep **current press shifts** and save fresh surplus wages.

feel: **Anxious** about current finances, less sharply about distant robots.

fieldNote: His **2026 press work** is certain, while post-2036 action requires continued employment and actual rosters.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture troubles you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture would put our mortgage at risk before I could qualify as a setter. A written staffing timetable, a funded paid safe apprenticeship place and posted reachable work at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Anything else I should have asked?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the children see when their parents lose paid shifts. My football team needs adults who can still show up on Tuesday.

headlineQuote: My football team needs adults who can still show up on Tuesday.
portrait: **Adam**, 43, feeds and checks a washing-machine stamping press and holds a vocational certificate earned before his years on the line.
His **school-cleaner partner**, two children, mortgage, low operator pay and reserve below one month make paid time critical.
He uses **AI occasionally** for football coaching and accepts proven work tools after safe practical instruction.
He seeks **funded setter training** and actual posted work, while fast press robots threaten most feeding hours.
biggestWorry: **Fast press robots** could take most feeding shifts before he qualifies for a paid setter vacancy.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing timetable**, offered funded paid safe training and reachable posted jobs paying household bills would help.
